{"id": "82:8/q20", "question": "Is divine speech here understood literally or metaphorically by some interpreters?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "82:8/q20/p1", "position": "Some say God's utterance is a production of meanings rather than real speech and treat much Quranic speech metaphorically.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports their analogy of saying a leaning wall ‘spoke.’ The note does not supply his own argument on this specific claim."}]}
{"id": "82:8/q21", "question": "What principles do the cited discussions of images, comparison, and figurative attribution give?", "turns_on": "These are distinct rhetorical accounts in cited discussions, not opposing readings of the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "82:8/q21/p1", "position": "Representation presents one image through another, while explicit simile presents two; abstract likeness needs a sensory model.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī uses a mirror versus direct sight, the moon's physical distance and near light for status and generosity, a directly seen flower, and a branch whose borrowed quality vanishes when comparison ends."}, {"id": "82:8/q21/p2", "position": "Poetic wonder can assert an impossible sight as fact; a broad shared device leaves each specific image distinct.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī discusses two suns, suns rising from beloveds' homes without an east, a walking moon, and embracing lions. He says specific wonders prevent a charge of plagiarism; a reverse technique transfers a subtle feature of the comparison's source to its target so simile or metaphor seems to disappear."}, {"id": "82:8/q21/p3", "position": "A complete metaphor would lend a name its full literal use; naming Zayd a lion does not transfer ‘lion’ without restriction.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī compares metaphor to lending clothing for full use; ‘Zayd’ restricts ‘lion,’ while ‘I meant a gazelle’ retains the animal noun's ordinary sense."}, {"id": "82:8/q21/p4", "position": "Figurative attribution presupposes a real bearer or agent behind the attributed property or action.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says a man's courage as lion-like first presupposes courage in the lion; a knife cutting or sword killing presupposes the wielder; a prince's building or minting presupposes workers. He excludes the disbelievers' literal claim that time destroys, citing 45:24."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q01", "question": "What is the spring called Tasnim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q01/p1", "position": "A spring or drink of Paradise called Tasnim, esteemed as its finest or highest drink.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani says ʿayn may denote a Paradise drink or spring and compares 76:6. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kur'an Yolu say this verse identifies the Tasnim of the preceding verse as a spring. Abu Salih calls it the noblest drink; Ibn ʿAbbas calls it the highest, and Ibn ʿAtiyya's report calls it the finest. Study Quran cites most commentators for its purity and nobility. Al-Nahhas reports Mujahid's derivation from elevation: elevated water, a raised grave, and a camel's hump; Elmalılı derives the name from raising like a hump and applies it to a high fountain."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q02", "question": "Where does the spring originate?", "turns_on": "The reported origin: Eden, Paradise's upper reaches, or beneath the Throne.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q02/p1", "position": "It comes from Eden, the core of Paradise.", "reasons": "Muqatil describes Eden as Paradise's core. Hudhayfa locates the spring in Eden; al-Qurtubi associates the foremost drinkers with Eden."}, {"id": "83:28/q02/p2", "position": "It descends from the upper or highest part of Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak says it flows from Paradise's highest part and no spring there is more honored. Al-Zajjaj describes its descent from the chambers; al-Tabari and al-Kalbi say it flows down upon the Garden's people. Elmalılı transmits al-Kalbi's account."}, {"id": "83:28/q02/p3", "position": "It flows from beneath the Throne.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says this is what they were told; al-Qurtubi adds that Hasan's mursal reports say the same."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q03", "question": "How does the spring reach the drinkers?", "turns_on": "Whether the account merely describes descent or specifies an airborne, measured delivery into vessels.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q03/p1", "position": "It descends or flows down to them from above.", "reasons": "Muqatil says it descends from Eden. Al-Zajjaj says it wafts toward the people from the chambers. Al-Tabari concludes that it flows down from above. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi place its downward flow above the drinkers, as Elmalılı also reports."}, {"id": "83:28/q03/p2", "position": "It flows through the air and fills each vessel in a measured amount.", "reasons": "Qatada says God's power suspends the flow in the air: it stops when a vessel fills, spills no drop on the ground, and removes the need to draw water. Elmalılı reports a similar aerial flow that pours enough into each vessel and elevates the elevated drinkers."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q04", "question": "Why is ʿaynan accusative?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted verb of praise or giving drink, circumstantial relation to a definite name, Tasnim's verbal derivation and tanwin, or reversed construction governs the accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q04/p1", "position": "It is an accusative of praise or specification, with an understood 'I mean a spring'.", "reasons": "Basran grammarians, Muhammad ibn Yazid as transmitted by Ali ibn Sulayman, al-Mubarrad, al-Zamakhshari, and later authors supply an omitted aʿni. Muhammad ibn Yazid says only this analysis works. Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Qurtubi call it praise; Bursevi and Tabataba'i include specification. Alusi contrasts this with al-Zajjaj's circumstantial analysis."}, {"id": "83:28/q04/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative from the definite Tasnim.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj makes Tasnim definite and ʿaynan indefinite. Al-Nahhas treats Tasnim as a feminine proper water name given tanwin by construing it as masculine water, and calls ʿaynan jāriyan circumstantial; he prefers the proper-name premise. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, and al-Samin report the analysis. Alusi says it can work if specified by the following clause or interpreted adjectivally. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls this far-fetched; al-Samin objects that Tasnim is a proper name for a concrete thing."}, {"id": "83:28/q04/p3", "position": "It is the object of an implied yusqawn, 'they are given a spring to drink'.", "reasons": "Basran grammarians posit an omitted yusqawn; al-Zajjaj glosses this as drinking from a spring. Al-Akhfash is reported by al-Nahhas, al-Wahidi, al-Qurtubi, and al-Samin. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls the proposed yusqawn analysis far-fetched."}, {"id": "83:28/q04/p4", "position": "It is governed by Tasnim taken as a verbal noun, or by an implied construction involving an indefinite spring.", "reasons": "Al-Farra offers an indefinite spring apposed to Tasnim and a welling-water construction, both yielding accusative; he cites 90:14, 77:25, and 5:95. Kufan grammarians posit an indefinite ʿayn after min Tasnim, then the accusative after tanwin, citing 90:15 and 77:25. Al-Nahhas reports al-Farra's 90:14–15 analogy. Ibn ʿAtiyya allows Tasnim as governing verbal noun; al-Qurtubi reports al-Farra's governing-object analysis. Al-Wahidi, on derivation from sanam, calls it causal and cites the hungry-day orphan verse."}, {"id": "83:28/q04/p5", "position": "It is explained by reversing the phrase as 'Tasnim, a spring'.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas records this fourth parsing without further argument."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q05", "question": "What does the bāʾ in yashrabu bihā convey?", "turns_on": "Whether bāʾ is partitive, extra, causal or instrumental, or locative; also whether yashrabu carries an added sense of quenching or mixing.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q05/p1", "position": "They drink from the spring; bāʾ has the sense 'from'.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives this as one reading; al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, and al-Nasafi gloss it explicitly. Al-Wahidi's direct drinking and al-Biqaʿi's reported direct spring drinking fit this sense. Al-Baydawi compares 76:6. Ibn ʿAshur attributes partitive bāʾ to al-Asmaʿi, al-Farisi, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Malik, and Kufan grammarians, but finds the partitive explanation unclear since Arabic normally uses bāʾ with drink. Islahi rejects this as vague and redundant because Tasnim has already been named as the source."}, {"id": "83:28/q05/p2", "position": "The bāʾ is extra, so the verb means 'they drink it'.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba also allows the spring as direct object. Ibn ʿAtiyya cites Abu Dhuʾayb's line with sharibna bi-māʾ al-baḥr; al-Biqaʿi? No: al-Samin, Bursevi, and Alusi state the extra-bāʾ option. Ibn ʿAshur cites the same Abu Dhuʾayb line about clouds drinking sea water and rising. Elmalılı proposes the fountain itself as the nearest's wine."}, {"id": "83:28/q05/p3", "position": "They are refreshed, satisfied, or delighted by the spring.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash includes the sense of being refreshed; al-Samin reads yashrabu with yurwa, quenching. Alusi lists satisfaction, enjoyment, and sufficiency. Elmalılı proposes satiety and delight through Tasnim."}, {"id": "83:28/q05/p4", "position": "The bāʾ marks mixing: they drink nectar by means of Tasnim as its blend.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi takes bāʾ as instrument or cause of the mixture. Ibn ʿAshur gives it causal force, with yashrabu including 'mix', and cites 83:27. Alusi lists mixing but questions it. Elmalılı notes the blended-drink rendering may appear natural, yet says it obscures the nearest's distinction and special tie to Tasnim."}, {"id": "83:28/q05/p5", "position": "They drink the nectar beside the spring; bāʾ marks accompaniment or location.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur supplies an omitted object, the nectar, and has the drinkers gathered around the spring; he suggests this is what the grammarians meant by bāʾ. Islahi makes bāʾ locative, comparing

{"id": "83:28/q06", "question": "How do the brought-near drink Tasnim compared with others?", "turns_on": "Whether the nearest receive Tasnim unmixed or as a blend, and whether those below them share any Tasnim.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q06/p1", "position": "They drink Tasnim pure and unmixed; the righteous or other Garden dwellers receive it blended into their drink.", "reasons": "This is transmitted from Abdullah or Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih, Qatada, Masruq, Hudhayfa, Hasan, Malik ibn al-Harith, and Muqatil; al-Tabari calls it the view of most exegetes and adopts it. Variants name recipients the companions of the right, the righteous, those below the nearest, or all other Garden people. Masruq says the blend sweetens their cups; Hudhayfa says it flows from Eden to them. Al-Baydawi says pure drink suits those occupied only with God; al-Tabatabaʿi sees Tasnim's superiority in 83:27. Elmalılı prefers this transmitted distinction; Samarraʾi says reward matches devotion."}, {"id": "83:28/q06/p2", "position": "The brought-near drink wine or nectar blended with Tasnim.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the close ones of Eden drink wine mixed with its water. Ibn ʿAshur takes the near ones as mixing nectar with Tasnim under the causal bāʾ, as 83:27 says; this does not specify whether others have access. Elmalılı reports the reading that they drink from Tasnim while blending it with sealed nectar, but finds that blended rendering unable to explain their special distinction."}, {"id": "83:28/q06/p3", "position": "Even blended Tasnim is reserved for the nearest; lower-ranking righteous people cannot drink it.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says the nearest drink the spring's blend while others have no access to the spring itself. Elmalılı reports a view under which the nearest cannot drink it pure either."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q07", "question": "Who are the muqarrabūn?", "turns_on": "Whether nearness denotes a higher human rank, all the righteous, or angels.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q07/p1", "position": "They are the foremost people brought near to God, a rank above the righteous companions of the right.", "reasons": "Most commentators distinguish the two groups, as Abu Hayyan and Alusi report. Elmalılı invokes the hierarchy of 56:10–11, the nearest witnessing the record in 83:21, and a saying contrasting the two ranks; he rejects treating the labels as synonyms. Alusi says the nearest are absorbed in God's love; al-Biqaʿi says God draws them near. Qashani characterizes the perfected, arrived near ones as steadfast in detailed realization."}, {"id": "83:28/q07/p2", "position": "The near ones and the righteous are synonymous labels for all the blessed in Paradise.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi report this minority identification. Ibn ʿAshur identifies the brought-near here with the righteous, saying those who drink the water are themselves brought near. Elmalılı rejects synonymy because it misses the distinction and force of the verse."}, {"id": "83:28/q07/p3", "position": "They are angels, the servants nearest to God's honor.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi explicitly identifies the muqarrabun with angels brought near to divine honor."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q08", "question": "What spiritual meaning is drawn from their drink?", "turns_on": "The spiritual contrast may concern pure vision versus mixed attention, the scene of intimacy, or distinctions among stations.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q08/p1", "position": "Pure Tasnim represents unalloyed knowledge, love, and vision of God; mixed drink represents attention also to created delights.", "reasons": "Bursevi calls Tasnim knowledge and love of God and joy in seeing His face, contrasting pure with mixed love. Elmalılı reports Razi's graded rivers: Tasnim is knowledge and vision of God, while sealed nectar is contemplation of creation. Study Quran reports Razi's view that the near ones see only God, whereas the people of the right also attend to created pleasures. Al-Baydawi says the nearest occupied themselves only with God; Alusi similarly cites absorption in divine love. Al-Sulami reports that attributes alone do not bring all to witness the Essence, whereas the near ones bear Essence and attributes."}, {"id": "83:28/q08/p2", "position": "Their drinking depicts intimate nearness to and beholding of God.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti says they drink pure while witnessing the beloved. Al-Jurayri locates them on the carpet of nearness, amid intimacy and gardens of holiness, drinking a cup of contentment while beholding God. Al-Thaʿlabi relays al-Hariri and al-Wasiti's image of closeness, intimacy, contentment, and witnessing."}, {"id": "83:28/q08/p3", "position": "The different drink names mark distinct spiritual stations even among the near ones.", "reasons": "Qashani says Tasnim's near ones stand by God in detailed steadfastness and realize unity of Essence, while 'servants of God' and kafur signal subjugation, annihilation, and undifferentiated unity."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q09", "question": "How does this verse connect to other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes point to different textual connections: the immediate Tasnim clause, an analogous spring, unseen delights, or the hierarchy of ranks.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q09/p1", "position": "It clarifies the Tasnim named as the blend in 83:27.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur and Kur'an Yolu say 83:28 identifies that spring. Tabataba'i calls the drinking clause an explanation of Tasnim and uses 83:27 to infer the superior pure drink. Ibn ʿAshur also cites 83:27 for the alternative blending parse."}, {"id": "83:28/q09/p2", "position": "The spring recalls the drink of God's servants in 76:5–6.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi applies the same discussion of bāʾ as in 76:6. Asad connects the two drinks; al-Damghani uses 76:6 to illustrate ʿayn as a Paradise spring. Islahi compares the riverside drinking image with 76:6."}, {"id": "83:28/q09/p3", "position": "The spring belongs with the Garden's unseen delights in 32:17.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi makes this explicit connection."}, {"id": "83:28/q09/p4", "position": "The higher drink follows the verse's and al-Waqiʿa's distinction between the nearest and the righteous.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites 83:21, where the nearest witness the record, and 56:10–11 for their higher rank. Study Quran lists 56:8, 27, 38, 90–91, 74:39, and 90:18 for the companions of the right. Samarraʾi compares 83:18, 25, 27 and says the higher reward matches greater devotion."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q10", "question": "What does the spring scene contribute to the passage's account of reward?", "turns_on": "The comments either explain the graded drink or describe the quality of Paradise's blessings generally.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q10/p1", "position": "The scene shows a higher reward for the brought-near, fitting their higher rank and devotion.", "reasons": "Elmalılı finds an ascending sequence from sealed nectar to Tasnim, parallel to the nearest above the righteous. Tabataba'i says pure Tasnim demonstrates the spring's superiority and the nearest's rank. Samarraʾi says the mixed and pure drinks match their devotion. Islahi says the pure wine is properly enjoyed beside a river and contrasts its etiquette with worldly wine."}, {"id": "83:28/q10/p2", "position": "The Garden's blessings form a life of peace, happiness, and virtue without worldly harms.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu specifies the absence of envy, conflict, unhappiness, injustice, illness, grief, and similar harms."}]}
{"id": "83:28/q11", "question": "How does this passage move between the righteous and the wicked?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the passage's transition or the explanation of the criminals' fate.", "positions": [{"id": "83:28/q11/p1", "position": "After describing the faithful's afterlife fate, it turns to worldly and final conditions of the faithful and fraudulent.", "reasons": "Islahi says 83:18–28 describes the loyal, faithful, and God-fearing. Elmalılı says that after giving the fraudulent and righteous their due afterlife fates, the passage turns to their conditions in this life and the next."}, {"id": "83:28/q11/p2", "position": "The criminals' punishment includes believers' satisfaction at their enemies' fate.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says the criminals wasted worldly life, lost what truly benefits them, and become the object of believers' satisfaction."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q01", "question": "Who is the human being addressed?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular address is universal, occasioned by a named person, or restricted to an individual or group.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q01/p1", "position": "Humanity generally, each accountable person.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says singular address can include a collective and cites 39:8; in another work he invokes God's forming people in varied appearances (30:22). Al-Tabrisi specifies every accountable descendant of Adam; al-Bursevi includes believers, unbelievers, and sinners. Al-Biqa'i says the singular treats humanity as a kind before each individual is discussed. Al-Tabataba'i grounds universality in God's universal lordship. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the warning especially targets conceited people absorbed in worldly life; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it chiefly warns resurrection-denying polytheists while reminding and reassuring believers. Abu Hayyan says a named occasion still leaves the wording general."}, {"id": "84:6/q01/p2", "position": "Al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies him; Abu Hayyan adds that he disputed resurrection with his brother Abū Salama, while the wording applies generally. Ibn ʿĀshūr records spelling variation and allows a named man to be the occasion or the intended addressee."}, {"id": "84:6/q01/p3", "position": "Ubayy ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan describes him as pursuing worldly gain, harming the Messenger, and persisting in disb

{"id": "84:6/q03", "question": "What does kadhḥ or kādiḥ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the root is understood through toil and scratching, return, walking, or its comparison with biting.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q03/p1", "position": "Strenuous, persistent work or exertion, in worldly or otherworldly life and in good or evil.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and al-Qurṭubī include earning a livelihood. Al-Zajjāj, Abū ʿUbayda, al-Qurṭubī, al-Tabrisī, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samīn cite Ibn Muqbil's akdaḥ for livelihood; al-Qurṭubī, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samīn cite another poem. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds intensity and speed and a poem about laboring through life. Al-Tabrisī compares the effort marks on a bull's hide; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abu Hayyan, al-Bursevī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connect it with scratching skin and effort that leaves a mark. Al-Layth defines it as one's good or evil work. Ibn ʿĀshūr says its original root sense is uncertain, while al-Rāghib defines exhausting work. Al-Qāshānī includes good and evil deeds."}, {"id": "84:6/q03/p2", "position": "Return to the Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss that one inevitably returns to the Lord and that kadhḥ means return."}, {"id": "84:6/q03/p3", "position": "Walking toward the Lord.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this as another possible sense of kādiḥ, with a different syntactic result for ilā."}, {"id": "84:6/q03/p4", "position": "A sense related to biting with the teeth.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports al-Rāghib's comparison with kadm and al-Khalīl's distinction that kadhḥ is less than kadm."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q04", "question": "What does the person's striving toward the Lord consist of or lead to?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase describes deeds done for God, all human toil as a journey, or the final meeting as its immediate endpoint.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q04/p1", "position": "Every person works through deeds, good or evil, and thereby advances toward the Lord and an account.", "reasons": "Muqātil says one meets God bearing deeds. Tustarī, al-Qushayrī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn Kathīr, al-Bursevī and al-Kurʾān Yolu describe work, judgment, and corresponding outcomes. Al-Tabrisī specifies life's hardships and accountable descendants of Adam. Ibn ʿĀshūr says successive daily work reaches tomorrow and finally death. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the servant is owned and governed by God and accountable for choices. Al-Qāshānī mentions exertion in good or evil acts. Al-Iṣlāḥī describes an unbroken journey from birth through changing states to death, irrespective of status. Asad emphasizes sorrow, pain, drudgery and worry for everyone."}, {"id": "84:6/q04/p2", "position": "The person performs work for the Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, with Qatāda in al-Baghawī, explain the work as deeds for God; al-Zajjāj reports this tafsīr, as does al-Suyūṭī's collection."}, {"id": "84:6/q04/p3", "position": "Life's toil moves one toward meeting the Lord at death and thereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī calls the destination death. Al-Bursevī speaks of death and subsequent states; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains how daily effort ends with death and return to God. Al-Qāshānī says every breath advances one swiftly through death. Asad says earthly toil ends at resurrection; al-Iṣlāḥī says this is the purpose of life's journey."}, {"id": "84:6/q04/p4", "position": "The person is carried inexorably toward meeting God and his appointed fate.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī frames this as rebuke and notes that right-hand recipients receive an easy, happy reckoning; Kurʾān Yolu says no one lives forever and God alone calls all to account."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q05", "question": "How does ilā work in 'toward your Lord'?", "turns_on": "How to construe the preposition and its governing expression.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q05/p1", "position": "It retains its directional sense: striving leads to or ends at meeting God.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisī prefers this construction and compares tabattal ilayhi (73:8), turning from creation or desiring God. Ibn ʿĀshūr says ilā marks the action's endpoint and makes kādiḥ the predicate of inna on the striving sense; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it gives the expression a journey sense."}, {"id": "84:6/q05/p2", "position": "Ilā has the sense of lām, 'for'.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisī reports this alternative grammatical view."}, {"id": "84:6/q05/p3", "position": "Ilā attaches to an omitted expression: one labors for oneself and arrives at the Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisī reports this possible construction."}, {"id": "84:6/q05/p4", "position": "With kādiḥ meaning 'walking,' the ilā phrase is an adverbial adjunct.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts this with his striving parse, where the phrase is a predicate."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q06", "question": "What is the grammatical force of kadhan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q06/p1", "position": "It is an emphatic accusative verbal noun or cognate object.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls it a verbal noun with emphatic force; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an accusative cognate object emphasizing kādiḥ and says the striving is unavoidable."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q07", "question": "How is famulāqīhi connected grammatically to the preceding clause?", "turns_on": "Whether fa coordinates a predicate or clause, introduces an elided predicate, or relates to the conditional; al-Naḥḥās also records an inflectional explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q07/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with kādiḥ or the preceding sentence, with a causal sequence.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the fa may coordinate with kādiḥ and that the causal relation is evident. {"id": "84:6/q08", "question": "Whom or what does the pronoun in famulāqīhi mean one meets?", "turns_on": "The pronoun's antecedent and whether meeting deeds is literal, metonymic for recompense, or a meeting with their record.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q08/p1", "position": "The Lord Himself, who judges and recompenses the person.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports this tafsīr; Abū Isḥāq, most exegetes cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Ibn ʿĀshūr take the pronoun this way. Al-Tabrisī says God alone judges. Al-Bayḍāwī makes the toil clause parenthetical and links meeting God with recompense. Ibn Kathīr says meeting God and one's deeds are compatible. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes a state with no screen from God's sole judgment; Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes inna to stress that none escapes."}, {"id": "84:6/q08/p2", "position": "One's work, labor, or deed, including its consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī report this; al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz places the meeting at Resurrection. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this can mean its good or bad reward. Al-Tabrisī says calling recompense 'the deed' magnifies its importance. Al-Samīn reports Ibn ʿAṭiyya's pronoun-to-effort parse. Ibn Kathīr cites the attributed saying to Jābir, 'act as you wish, for you will meet your deeds,' and Ibn ʿAbbās's report; al-Suyūṭī and Study Quran report similar Ibn ʿAbbās material, the latter citing 99:6–8. Al-Qāshānī notes possible harmful consequences. Ibn Kathīr says the Lord and deed readings are compatible."}, {"id": "84:6/q08/p3", "position": "The recompense or punishment for one's deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī chooses reward as the intended encounter; al-Qushayrī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya specify good for good and evil for evil. Ibn Kathīr says the Lord reading entails recompense too. Al-Bursevī says no one escapes the outcome of worldly acts."}, {"id": "84:6/q08/p4", "position": "The record of one's deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī argues that the work itself is over and the following verse speaks of receiving the book."}]}

{"id": "84:6/q10", "question": "How is kādiḥ ilā rabbika parsed in relation to inna?", "turns_on": "Whether kādiḥ means striving or walking.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q10/p1", "position": "Kādiḥ, with ilā marking the destination, is the predicate of inna.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the preposition points to the action's endpoint, meeting God, when kādiḥ means striving."}, {"id": "84:6/q10/p2", "position": "If kādiḥ means walking, the ilā phrase is an adverbial adjunct.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this as the alternative parsing."}]}

{"id": "84:6/q12", "question": "What conduct does the verse urge?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary exhortations about how to respond to inevitable striving.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q12/p1", "position": "Direct one's inevitable effort toward obedience and deeds that bring a good outcome.", "reasons": "Tustarī urges examining whether one's striving suits the Garden and nearness or the Fire and distance; he reports Kamhas's forty years of tears after taking a piece of a neighbor's wall for a guest who had eaten fish bought for one daniq. Qatāda says weak human striving should be made obedience if possible, with help only from God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says life's speed makes this a warning to act righteously. Al-Bursevī urges saving actions and avoiding ruin, shame and disgrace. Maybudī urges mindfulness as each moment brings one nearer God."}, {"id": "84:6/q12/p2", "position": "Act despite predestination: each person is eased toward what he was created to do.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī reports the Prophet's reply to a question about how to act after pens had dried and destinies were decreed."}, {"id": "84:6/q12/p3", "position": "Live and love mindful of death and separation, and act mindful of meeting deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Jābir's saying attributed to Gabriel addressing Muḥammad: live as you wish because you will die, love as you wish because you will part, and act as you wish because you will meet your deeds."}, {"id": "84:6/q12/p4", "position": "A remorseful person awaits mercy, a self-admiring one condemnation, and each worker what was sent ahead.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī cites this hadith to explain the outcome of deeds."}]}
{"id": "84:6/q13", "question": "How does the verse ground accountability and resurrection?", "turns_on": "The argument from God's lordship and justice, and the scope of recompense for deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q13/p1", "position": "Universal lordship makes each person's return, judgment, and recompense necessary.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues from lordship to servitude, responsibility, return, accounting, and recompense; God's ownership means a servant should will and do only what God commands. Al-Iṣlāḥī calls accountability the purpose for which the world was created and invokes innate justice and the world's purpose for the final separation. Al-Biqa'i says each person's striving is judged, with different outcomes for disbelievers and Muslims. Kurʾān Yolu says only God calls people to account."}, {"id": "84:6/q13/p2", "position": "Human effort is unavoidable and ends in a fitting good or evil outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī and al-Baghawī say good meets good and evil meets evil. Al-Bursevī says there is no escape from recompense; Elmalılı says life's exertion ends in a painful or pleasant outcome from God. {"id": "84:6/q14", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding passage and other sūrahs?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is with the immediate judgment scene, a preceding or another sūrah, or related return language.", "positions": [{"id": "84:6/q14/p1", "position": "The cosmic opening leads to every person's deeds, record, judgment, and two outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī links the sky splitting to seeing good or evil sent ahead. Al-Qurṭubī points to the next verse's book-taking when identifying what is met."}, {"id": "84:6/q14/p2", "position": "Al-Inshiqāq continues al-Muṭaffifīn's judgment of those who denied resurrection and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says allies receive reward and enemies punishment after denying their Creator-King. {"id": "84:13/q09", "question": "Why is his worldly happiness blameworthy?", "turns_on": "Which neglected duty or belief the sources emphasize: obedience and restraint, resurrection, or concern for others and family.", "positions": [{"id": "84:13/q09/p1", "position": "It was bound up with sin, self-indulgence, and limiting concern to this life.", "reasons": "Tabari names defiance of God's command and sins; Jishumi condemns worldly pleasure, short worldly aspirations, and turning from the afterlife as ending in regret. {"id": "84:13/q10", "question": "What becomes of his worldly happiness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:13/q10/p1", "position": "It is reversed by humiliation, grief, and punishment in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Muqatil says God will humble the once-honored man at resurrection. {"id": "84:13/q11", "question": "How does his joy contrast with the believer's experience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:13/q11/p1", "position": "The believer bears concern in the world and gains joy and reunion in the Hereafter; the heedless person's course is reversed.", "reasons": "Tabrisi contrasts the believer's religious concern and lasting joy with brief joy and unending grief. {"id": "84:14/q01", "question": "Who is the person called 'he'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q01/p1", "position": "The disbeliever who receives his record behind his back; Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies this group as polytheists.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies him by the record handed behind his back; al-Zajjāj calls him the disbeliever; Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts these polytheists with right-hand recipients, the believers (84:7–15). {"id": "84:14/q02", "question": "What does the pronoun in 'indeed he' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q02/p1", "position": "It can belittle the person it denotes.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī compares pronouns used of Satan as an evident enemy, of Satan and his tribe seeing humans unseen, and of this person who assumes he will not return."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q03", "question": "What does ẓanna mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether ẓann retains its ordinary sense of supposition or denotes certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q03/p1", "position": "He reckoned or supposed that he would not return.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says ẓanna keeps its ordinary meaning. Damghānī gives reckoning or supposing as a sense, and Fatḥ al-Raḥmān explicitly denies that it means certainty."}, {"id": "84:14/q03/p2", "position": "It means certainty.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports al-Fanārī's interpretation from his Tafsīr al-Fātiḥa. {"id": "84:14/q04", "question": "How does 'an' and its clause function after ẓanna?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause occupies both objects of ẓanna or only one.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q04/p1", "position": "Lightened an and its clause fill both object positions of ẓanna.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās assigns the clause to the two objects. {"id": "84:14/q06", "question": "What force does 'lan' add to the person's expectation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q06/p1", "position": "Its emphatic negation expresses the denier's firm certainty that he will not return to life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly attributes the force of certainty to lan."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q07", "question": "What did he believe would not happen when he would not 'yaḥūr'?", "turns_on": "Whether the denied return is specified as resurrection before God, a reversal of worldly fortune, or a supposition about God's knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q07/p1", "position": "He believed he would not return to God or rise after death for judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Mujāhid, Sufyān's lexical gloss, and later exegetes give return, resurrection, or both. Al-Rāghib, reported by al-Samīn and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, specifies return to life or resurrection; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls this a context-fixed Islamic sense.
